sites.name: North Beach
sites.description: Eilat's main city-front beach at the very head of the gulf, fronted by seagrass beds that shelter stingrays and spotted eagle rays alongside lionfish, pufferfish and wrasse -- an easy, gently sloping sandy entry that's one of the best pure snorkeling spots in town, not just a dive site. Visibility is best in the morning before the wind picks up, and it gets some angling and small-boat traffic, so watch for lines and props; on days with a strong north wind it's best not to swim too far south along the beach.
sites.pro_tip: Go early -- visibility drops through the day as the wind builds, and it's the best window to spot rays cruising the seagrass before boat traffic picks up.

sites.name: Sun Boat
sites.description: A former liveaboard deliberately sunk in 2010 about 300 yards off HaDatiyim Beach, just south of North Beach; it stands upright on the sand with its bow facing north, reachable by a long surface swim or snorkel from shore. The distance from the beach and depth over most of the sandy approach make it a better fit for confident swimmers and divers than first-timers.
sites.pro_tip: The snorkel/dive entry is marked by a yellow buoy -- the wreck sits about 16 yards to its left, not straight out, which is the detail people miss on their first attempt.

sites.name: Dolphin Reef
sites.description: An open-enclosure marine park south of the city where a resident pod of bottlenose dolphins, originally brought from a defunct Black Sea dolphinarium, has lived semi-wild for decades and comes and goes freely into the open gulf. Shallow, easy diving and snorkeling with a real chance of a close dolphin encounter, alongside typical schooling reef fish.

sites.name: Katza (EAPC Beach)
sites.description: A former Eilat-Ashkelon Pipeline Company beach closed to the public for roughly 50 years and only reopened in 2017; its old pipeline support pillars are now thickly encrusted with soft coral, hard coral and sponges and host a real diversity of fish and invertebrates. Maximum depth reaches 30m but the best views are much shallower, and it's suited to both snorkeling and diving right off the sand.
sites.pro_tip: Come at sunrise or sunset -- the resident bottlenose dolphins from neighbouring Dolphin Reef often wander down the coast past Katza at low light, and dawn dives here have a very good track record of a dolphin encounter.

sites.name: Princess Beach
sites.description: The southernmost beach on Israel's coast, right by the Egyptian border, with thriving shallow coral patches and excellent visibility; a favorite easy snorkeling spot for green chromis, yellowtail surgeonfish, lionfish, parrotfish, butterflyfish and clownfish. Entry is straight off the sand or via two old piers that are themselves worth exploring.
sites.pro_tip: The two old piers are easier entry points than the open sand, and they're interesting snorkeling in their own right -- fish tend to stack up in their shade.

sites.name: Coral Beach Nature Reserve
sites.description: Israel's only shore-accessible coral reef and the northernmost shallow-water coral reef in the world, protecting a 1.2km strip of densely packed hard and soft coral just off the beach. Bridges built out over the reef let snorkelers and divers reach the seaward side without touching coral, and the shallow section is Israel's most popular snorkeling spot -- turtles, schooling reef fish and the reserve's namesake corals are the draw.
sites.pro_tip: Use the bridges to reach the outer reef face rather than swimming over the shallow coral table directly -- it's both the routine local etiquette and the better way to avoid contact with the reef.

sites.name: Moses Rock
sites.description: A single large coral head near the reserve's northern entrance, close enough to the surface to be a classic beginner and snorkel-adjacent dive, packed with an outsized amount of biodiversity for its size. Usually dived alongside its neighbour Joshua Rock as the opening of a Nature Reserve dive.

sites.name: Joshua Rock
sites.description: Paired with Moses Rock at the start of the Nature Reserve, this second coral head marks the shallow entry point most Coral Beach dives begin from. A calm, low-current introduction to the reserve's reef life before continuing south toward deeper sites.

sites.name: Japanese Gardens
sites.description: A long, exceptionally well-preserved coral wall and slope at the southern end of the Nature Reserve, boat-access only and often called the most beautiful single dive site in Eilat; the coral wall keeps going well past recreational limits, so most operators cap the dive around 30-40m. Because it needs a boat and advance booking, it sees far fewer divers than the shore-accessible sites further north.
sites.pro_tip: Boat access and advance booking keep the crowds away here compared to Moses Rock and the Caves -- worth the extra logistics if you want the reserve's best coral without the shore-dive traffic.

sites.name: The Caves
sites.description: A shallow, roughly 100m reef strip at Lighthouse Beach threaded with small swim-through tunnels and packed with reef fish and critters; shallow and close to shore, it's one of Eilat's most popular training, first-dive and night-dive sites.
sites.pro_tip: The shallow depth here makes it forgiving for a night dive if you're newer to diving after dark -- easier buoyancy margin than the deeper sites further south.

sites.name: Eel Garden
sites.description: Eilat's own eel garden -- a distinct site from the one in Sharm el Sheikh -- entered through a narrow canyon around 9m that opens onto a broad sandy slope running down to about 18-20m, just north of the Almog Beach reserve fence near the Coral Beach Hotel. Named for its colony of garden eels swaying upright against the current at the bottom of the slope.
sites.pro_tip: Keep going past the eel colony to the near-flat reef section around 20m -- that's where thick barracuda schools regularly patrol, and most divers turn back too early to see them.

sites.name: Three Sisters
sites.description: Three coral formations roughly 100m apart in a north-south line on a sandy seabed south of Lighthouse Beach, each rising a few metres from the bottom; a relaxed, shallow site good for beginners, with moray eels, octopus and plenty of small tropical fish around the formations.

sites.name: The University
sites.description: A gentle sloping reef named for its proximity to the Interuniversity Institute for Marine Sciences (IUI), which runs ongoing coral restoration and cultivation plots along part of the site. An easy, low-current dive that doubles as a look at active coral research rather than just a reef.
sites.pro_tip: Ask your guide to point out the coral-planting research plots -- they're easy to swim past without noticing, but it's one of the only working coral restoration sites you can dive directly.

sites.name: Satil
sites.description: A 40m Israeli missile boat -- originally one of the vessels covertly taken from Cherbourg harbour in 1969 -- deliberately sunk in 1994 as an underwater museum roughly 70m offshore. It carries two memorial plaques for a soldier and a diving instructor, sits with its deck around 18-21m and keel near 22-24m, and is thickly grown with soft coral on its east side while the west side is more weed-covered.
sites.pro_tip: Circle both sides before you surface -- the west side is mostly seaweed while the east is properly coral-encrusted, and divers who only see one side miss half the wreck's character.

sites.name: Yatush Wreck
sites.description: A former Israeli Navy patrol vessel -- Yatush is Hebrew for "mosquito", and some older dive-shop material refers to this or a related sunk patrol boat as "the Mosquito" or "the Hawk" -- deliberately sunk off Eilat as an artificial reef and entered from Veranda Beach. It sits upright, stern around 24-26m and bow down to 30-32m, fully penetrable for wreck-certified divers, with wrasse, parrotfish, anthias, moray eels, lionfish and garden eels around the hull.
sites.pro_tip: Wreck penetration here is strictly cert-only and enforced -- come with the paperwork if you want to go inside, since dive centers will turn away uncertified divers at the door rather than bend the rule.

sites.name: Neptune's Tables
sites.description: One of the southernmost Eilat sites, close to the Taba border crossing, named for its large, very old table Acropora corals at depth; sometimes grouped with a neighbouring spot called Veronica. Recommended for Open Water-level divers and up, with plentiful reef life at varying depths around the tables.

sites.name: Paradise
sites.description: A deep, largely flat seabed near the Taba border carpeted in extensive, colourful soft and hard coral with a good diversity of reef animals; a deeper-water site for experienced divers rather than a wall or wreck. Note: the Satil wreck is also known locally by the nickname "Paradise", so confirm with your operator which site is meant.

sites.name: The Canyon
sites.description: Two notable underwater canyons cutting into the reef within the Nature Reserve's southern section, starting around 20m and dropping further; a good option for certified divers wanting more relief and structure than the open reef slopes nearby.

sites.name: Tamar Reef
sites.description: A shallow artificial reef built from perforated concrete structures designed to be colonised by coral and reef fish, sitting in only about 8m of water. A gentle, easy dive suited to beginners and popular for its slowly maturing artificial-reef coral growth.

sites.name: Dubek Pyramid
sites.description: An artificial pyramid structure built in the early 1990s in a busy sailing and water-sports area off the hotel strip, now colonised by red sponge coral and reef life. Its location under heavy surface boat traffic means it's usually dived from a boat rather than shore.

sites.name: Statue Garden
sites.description: An underwater sculpture garden -- also called the Sculpture Garden -- featuring works by artist Dan Rapoport, reachable by boat near the reserve's southern stretch; a newer addition to Eilat's dive-site roster combining art installations with reef growth.

sites.name: Underwater Restaurant
sites.description: The remains of a former underwater restaurant structure, its window frames still intact, now grown over with coral and home to resident reef fish; an easy, novelty shallow dive close to the city.

species.description: The larger of the two manta species, distinct from the reef manta ray seen further south at Tiran -- Eilat's manta encounters, including a documented surge of sightings and repeat individuals photo-matched across 2020, 2022 and 2025, are consistently of this bigger, more oceanic species rather than Mobula alfredi.
species.habitat: Open water off the reef edge
species.population_info: Endangered globally from targeted and bycatch fishing pressure elsewhere in its range; Gulf of Aqaba sightings are opportunistic rather than seasonal, but photo-ID has matched the same individuals returning in different years, suggesting at least some site fidelity to the gulf.
